claims.claim: micro:bit's published lesson plans embed paired 'support' and 'stretch' differentiation notes in each short lesson, so a single 45-60 minute session can scaffold struggling learners and extend advanced ones without a second plan.

For primary-aged (8-11) learners who struggle, micro:bit lessons rely on teacher-led scaffolding plus a step-by-step tutorial or a pre-built 'remix' project so they still reach the core forever-loop + show-string/icon outcome.

micro:bit lessons give advanced learners an 'Extend' phase with open-ended challenges (e.g. change the pause timing, add a second animation, or combine inputs) instead of capping the task, keeping one lesson open-ended at the top.

Within an if/then + shake + random lesson, stretch is delivered by remixing the core program (adding random outcomes or new gesture handlers) while the support tier keeps a single-branch if/then skeleton the pupil can complete.

CS-education guidance for primary block coding favours 'low floor, high ceiling' single-lesson tasks so every pupil meets the objective yet advanced pupils have room to extend - the same pattern micro:bit applies via its support/stretch notes.

The Techno Square repackaging of these micro:bit lessons dropped the upstream support/stretch differentiation (together with assessment and answer key), leaving a gap the kids-track intro unit must restore to serve mixed-ability 8-11 classrooms.
